summary: This Informational document describes Multiple Loss Ratio Search (MLRsearch), an alternative to the throughput test in RFC 2544. It aims to shorten search time, support several loss ratio goals, and make results more repeatable and comparable.

eli5.summary: Finding how much a pipe can carry by trying different amounts until too much spills, but smarter, so it takes less time and gives the same answer each time.

questions: how does mlrsearch improve on rfc 2544
why is throughput testing slow with binary search
subtitle: A faster, more reliable way to measure how much traffic a network can handle.

tldr.problem: RFC 2544 defined the standard way to test network device throughput, but the binary search method it describes is slow, produces unrepeatable results, and cannot handle modern software-based networking on commodity hardware or support tests with acceptable small amounts of packet loss.
tldr.mechanism: MLRsearch (Multiple Loss Ratio Search) introduces a new benchmarking methodology that uses multiple short trials instead of one long trial, searches for multiple loss-ratio goals simultaneously, applies conservative bounds to handle inconsistent results, and can handle noisy performance typical of software-based systems.
tldr.outcome: MLRsearch significantly reduces test duration while improving result repeatability and comparability, making it practical to thoroughly benchmark software networking functions. It remains compatible with RFC 2544 when configured with strict settings.

today: RFC 9971 was published in August 2026 as an Informational document. It provides a standardized methodology for network benchmarking that is particularly valuable for testing software-based network functions. The methodology is increasingly adopted in the industry for testing virtual network functions, software switches, and packet processing applications where RFC 2544's approach proved impractical.

sections.title: The Problem with RFC 2544 Testing
sections.content:
RFC 2544 defines the standard methodology for benchmarking network devices, including how to measure throughput: the maximum load at which zero frames are lost. It uses a binary search algorithm: start with upper and lower load bounds, test the midpoint, adjust bounds based on whether loss occurred, and repeat until the bounds are close enough.

However, this approach has several problems. First, it is slow: most trials are conducted far from the eventual result, wasting time on irrelevant measurements. Second, the requirement for 60-second trials at full precision prolongs the total search duration. Third, software-based networking (running on generic CPUs instead of specialized hardware) exhibits noisy performance with frequent unpredictable variations, making results spread widely and poorly repeatable. Fourth, throughput requires zero loss, but modern protocols tolerate low but non-zero loss; requiring absolute zero-loss is overly strict. Fifth, when trial results are inconsistent (higher load produces lower loss), the definition of throughput becomes ambiguous.
sections.eli5: The old way of testing had problems: it took too long, it didn't work well on software networks that are jumpy, and it required absolutely zero lost packets which is unrealistic.

sections.title: MLRsearch Overview and Key Innovations
sections.content:
MLRsearch (Multiple Loss Ratio Search) addresses these problems through several key enhancements. First, it allows multiple short trials per load instead of a single long trial, and tolerates a specified proportion of trials with higher loss. Second, it supports searching for multiple loss-ratio goals simultaneously, enabling a single test to find many different performance points (e.g., performance at 0% loss, at 0.5% loss, at 1% loss) in one search.

Third, MLRsearch handles inconsistent trial results conservatively: the reported lower bound is the largest load that is smaller than the smallest load with high loss. This prevents overoptimistic results when trials are noisy. Fourth, the methodology allows non-zero loss ratios as search goals, aligning with real-world operator needs. Fifth, MLRsearch provides configurable stopping conditions and balances search duration against precision.
sections.eli5: MLRsearch fixes the problems by doing many quick tests instead of fewer long ones, testing several acceptable loss amounts at once, being careful about noisy results, and letting you say "a tiny bit of loss is okay."

sections.title: Search Goals and Results
sections.content:
At the heart of MLRsearch is the Search Goal, which specifies what the search should find. Each goal has several parameters. Goal Loss Ratio is the target acceptable packet loss (e.g., 0% for strict or 0.5% for lenient). Goal Final Trial Duration is the minimum trial length that trials must reach before confirming a lower bound (typically 60 seconds). Goal Duration Sum controls how many total seconds of trials are needed (e.g., 60 seconds for one 60-second trial or 120 seconds to allow up to two 60-second trials). Goal Exceed Ratio is the tolerance for high-loss trials (e.g., 50% allows up to half the trials to exceed the loss target). Goal Width is the stopping condition (how close the bounds must be).

The search produces a Search Result for each goal, consisting of a Relevant Lower Bound (the highest load meeting the loss requirement), a Relevant Upper Bound (the lowest load exceeding the loss requirement), and a Conditional Throughput (the actual forwarding rate observed at the lower bound, accounting for realistic conditions like hard performance limits of network interfaces).
sections.eli5: A search goal is like a recipe: it says "I want to find the fastest speed where packet loss is no more than this amount, and I'm willing to run this many tests to find it." The result tells you the speed you found and how confident you are.

sections.title: Classifying Loads as Bounds
sections.content:
The core logic of MLRsearch is Load Classification, which determines whether a tested load qualifies as a lower bound or upper bound for a goal. Unlike RFC 2544's simple yes/no rule on a single long trial, MLRsearch classifies a load by analyzing all trials performed at that load, considering their duration and loss ratio.

Specifically, MLRsearch computes whether, given all observed trials and their durations, it is optimistically (best case) or pessimistically (worst case) likely that the load meets the goal. If the optimistic exceed ratio exceeds the goal's tolerance, the load is an upper bound (too high). If the pessimistic exceed ratio does not exceed the goal's tolerance, the load is a lower bound (good enough). Otherwise, the load is undecided (more trials needed). This approach handles noisy trial results gracefully: occasionally bad trials do not automatically disqualify a load if other trials at the same load were good.
sections.eli5: When you've done multiple tests at the same speed, MLRsearch counts the bad tests and the good tests, and decides whether that speed is acceptable based on how many good ones outnumber bad ones.

sections.title: Advantages and Implementation Flexibility
sections.content:
MLRsearch offers several practical advantages. Reduced test time is achieved through intelligent load selection and support for short trials. Improved repeatability comes from searching for performance near the noiseless end of the spectrum using multiple trials. Multi-goal support allows a single search to characterize performance across different loss tolerances. Flexibility in trial duration, loss tolerance, and stopping conditions allows implementations to trade off precision against speed according to their needs.

Importantly, MLRsearch is not a rigid standard but a methodology framework. The specification defines the terminology, architecture (Manager, Controller, Measurer components), and load classification logic, but leaves implementation details flexible. This allows future IETF benchmarking documents to define specific, comparable benchmarks by mandating particular search goal configurations. MLRsearch remains compatible with RFC 2544 when configured conservatively (60-second trials, zero loss, zero exceed ratio), but configurations can be less strict for faster, more practical testing.
sections.eli5: MLRsearch is flexible: you can make it strict to match old standards, or you can adjust settings to test faster and still get good information. It's a framework that different tests can use in different ways.

sections.title: Handling Noisy Software-Based Systems
sections.content:
A key motivation for MLRsearch is the DUT-in-SUT problem: when a Device Under Test (DUT) runs on shared commodity hardware (servers with generic CPUs), the entire System Under Test (SUT) experiences interference from the operating system, other software workloads, and CPU resource contention. This creates noise that causes trial results to fluctuate unpredictably, even when testing the same load twice.

MLRsearch models this noise as a spectrum: the DUT has an idealized noiseless performance at one end and increasingly noisy performance at the other. By using multiple trials and conservative bounds, MLRsearch estimates the noiseless end of the performance spectrum, improving repeatability. This is why goal attributes like Goal Exceed Ratio and multiple short trials matter: they filter out rare but extreme noise events and focus on typical observable performance. The Conditional Throughput metric accounts for hard performance limits (e.g., a network interface's maximum frame rate), reporting the actual forwarding rate observed rather than an inflated load value.
sections.eli5: Software tests are noisier because the computer is running other things at the same time. MLRsearch handles that by running many tests and ignoring the occasional really bad result, finding the true normal performance.
